concepts.label: The Consumer in the Marketplace
concepts.cardText: Individual consumers often find themselves in a weak position: when there is a complaint, the seller tries to shift all responsibility on to the buyer. Exploitation happens through unfair trade practices, such as shopkeepers weighing less, traders adding charges not mentioned before, or selling adulterated or defective goods. Markets do not work fairly when producers are few and powerful while consumers buy in small amounts and are scattered; large companies can manipulate the market and pass on false information through the media. A long battle with court cases was needed to make cigarette makers accept that their product could cause cancer. So rules and regulations are needed to protect consumers.
concepts.hint: Why is one buyer weak against a large company? Think of weights, extra charges, adulteration and false advertising.
concepts.probe: What are the various ways in which consumers are exploited in the market, and why are rules and regulations needed?
concepts.causeChain: Producers few and powerful, consumers small and scattered -> unfair trade practices and false information -> consumers exploited -> rules and regulations needed to protect consumers

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the imbalance between powerful producers and scattered consumers (and the resulting exploitation) to the need for rules and regulations to protect consumers.

concepts.label: The Consumer Movement and COPRA
concepts.cardText: The consumer movement arose out of consumers' dissatisfaction with unfair practices by sellers, when there was no legal system to protect them. Earlier, consumers were expected to be careful themselves; awareness created by organisations shifted the responsibility for quality on to sellers. In India, rampant food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration of food and edible oil gave birth to an organised consumer movement in the 1960s. Till the 1970s, consumer organisations mostly wrote articles and held exhibitions. The movement put pressure on business and government, and in 1986 the government enacted the Consumer Protection Act (COPRA), amended in 2019. Internationally, the UN adopted Guidelines for Consumer Protection in 1985.

concepts.causeChain: Dissatisfaction with unfair practices + no legal protection -> food shortages, hoarding, black marketing, adulteration in the 1960s -> organised consumer movement -> pressure on business and government -> COPRA 1986

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the pressure created by the consumer movement to the enactment of the Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) in 1986.

keyPoints.text: The consumer movement arose out of dissatisfaction of the consumers as many unfair practices were being indulged in by the sellers. There was no legal system available to consumers to protect them. It was presumed that it was the responsibility of consumers to be careful while buying; organisations created awareness, which shifted the responsibility of ensuring quality of goods and services on the sellers.

checks.criterion: Explains that the consumer movement arose from consumers' dissatisfaction with unfair practices by sellers, when there was no legal system to protect them.

keyPoints.text: In India, the consumer movement as a 'social force' originated with the necessity of protecting and promoting the interests of consumers against unethical and unfair trade practices. Rampant food shortages, hoarding, black marketing, adulteration of food and edible oil gave birth to the consumer movement in an organised form in the 1960s. Till the 1970s, consumer organisations were largely engaged in writing articles and holding exhibitions, and formed groups to look into malpractices in ration shops and overcrowding in road transport.
keyPoints.followUp: What problems in India led to the consumer movement becoming a social force?

checks.criterion: States that food shortages, hoarding, black marketing and adulteration gave birth to an organised consumer movement in India in the 1960s.
Mentions that until the 1970s consumer organisations mostly wrote articles, held exhibitions or watched ration shops and road transport.

keyPoints.text: The movement succeeded in bringing pressure on business firms as well as government to correct unfair business conduct. A major step taken in 1986 by the Indian government was the enactment of the Consumer Protection Act 1986, popularly known as COPRA. This Act was amended in 2019.
keyPoints.followUp: What major law did the consumer movement lead to in India?

checks.criterion: States that the Indian government enacted the Consumer Protection Act 1986 (COPRA), amended in 2019.

keyPoints.text: In 1985 the United Nations adopted the UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection, which became the foundation for the consumer movement at the international level. Today, Consumers International is an umbrella body of over 200 member organisations from over 100 countries.

checks.criterion: Mentions the UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection adopted in 1985.

concepts.label: Right to Safety
concepts.cardText: Reji Mathew, a Class IX student, was crippled for life after improper anaesthesia during a tonsil operation at a private clinic. The State Commission dismissed his father's complaint, but the National Commission held the hospital responsible for medical negligence and ordered it to pay compensation. Consumers have the right to be protected against the marketing of goods and delivery of services that are hazardous to life and property. Producers must strictly follow safety rules, as with the safety valve of a pressure cooker. Bad quality products still reach the market because supervision of these rules is weak and the consumer movement is not strong enough.

keyPoints.text: We as consumers have the right to be protected against the marketing of goods and delivery of services that are hazardous to life and property. Producers need to strictly follow the required safety rules and regulations; for example, pressure cookers have a safety valve which, if defective, can cause a serious accident.

concepts.label: Right to Information
concepts.cardText: Packaged goods show ingredients, price, batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date and the manufacturer's address; medicines show directions for use and side effects. These rules exist because consumers have the right to be informed about the particulars of goods and services they buy, so they can complain and ask for compensation or replacement if the product is defective. One can protest if a good is sold above the printed MRP (maximum retail price), and even bargain below it. In October 2005, the RTI (Right to Information) Act extended this right to government functions; Amritha, an engineering graduate, used it to learn her job result and got her call letter.

keyPoints.text: When you buy any commodity, you will find details given on the packing about ingredients used, price, batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date and the address of the manufacturer. Rules have been made so that the manufacturer displays this information because consumers have the right to be informed about the particulars of goods and services that they purchase.

concepts.label: Right to Choose
concepts.cardText: Abirami paid Rs 61,020 in advance for a two-year coaching course but left after one year because the teaching was poor; the institute refused a refund. The District Consumer Commission directed it to refund Rs 28,000, saying she had the right to choose. The State Commission upheld this, fined the institute Rs 25,000 for a frivolous appeal, ordered Rs 7000 as compensation and litigation cost, and barred institutions in the state from charging fees for the whole course in advance. Any consumer has the right to choose whether to continue receiving a service. The right to choice is denied when a shop sells toothpaste only with a toothbrush, or a gas dealer insists that you buy a stove with a new connection.

concepts.label: Right to Seek Redressal
concepts.cardText: Consumers have the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices and exploitation. If any damage is done to a consumer, she has the right to get compensation depending on the degree of damage. An easy and effective public system is needed for this. A consumer can file a complaint before the appropriate consumer forum on his or her own, with or without lawyers. Prakash's money order for his daughter's marriage never arrived; he filed a case in a district Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission and pleaded it himself. Today consumers, individually or as a group (a class action suit), can file complaints physically or online and attend through video conferencing.

keyPoints.text: Consumers have the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices and exploitation. concepts.label: Consumer Forums and the Three-Tier Commissions
concepts.cardText: The consumer movement has led to voluntary organisations called consumer forums or consumer protection councils. They guide consumers on how to file cases in the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions, often represent them there, and get government support for creating awareness; Residents' Welfare Associations also take up members' cases. Under COPRA, a three-tier quasi-judicial machinery was set up: the District Commission handles claims up to Rs 1 crore, the State Commission between Rs 1 crore and Rs 10 crore, and the National Commission claims above Rs 10 crore. A dismissed case can be appealed to the State and then the National Commission. So the Act gives consumers the right to represent in these commissions.

concepts.label: Becoming Well-Informed Consumers: ISI and Agmark
concepts.cardText: When consumers become conscious of their rights, they can make informed choices; this calls for the knowledge and skill to become a well-informed consumer. COPRA led to separate Departments of Consumer Affairs in central and state governments, which spread information through posters and television advertisements. Logos like ISI, Agmark, Hallmark and +F assure consumers of quality; producers may use them only if they follow quality standards. These standards are not compulsory for all producers, but certification is mandatory for products that affect health and safety or are of mass consumption, like LPG cylinders, food colours and additives, cement and packaged drinking water.

concepts.label: Taking the Consumer Movement Forward
concepts.cardText: India observes 24 December as National Consumers' Day, the day Parliament enacted COPRA in 1986, and is one of the countries with an exclusive authority for consumer redressal. There are more than 2000 consumer groups, but only about 50-60 are well organised. The redressal process is becoming cumbersome, expensive and time consuming: consumers often need lawyers, cash memos are not issued in most purchases so evidence is hard to gather, and most purchases are small retail sales. COPRA was amended in 2019: buying through the internet is now included, providers and manufacturers can be penalised or imprisoned, and mediation is encouraged. Awareness is spreading slowly, and consumer movements work only with consumers' active involvement.

concepts.probe: Critically examine the progress of the consumer movement in India.
concepts.causeChain: Progress: COPRA, National Consumers' Day, 2000+ groups, 2019 amendment; problems: cumbersome, costly, slow process, no cash memos, small purchases, weak enforcement -> movement effective only with consumers' active involvement

causeLinks.criterion: Connects the problems of the redressal process and slow awareness to the need for consumers' active involvement in the movement.

keyPoints.text: India has been observing 24 December as the National Consumers' Day, the day the Indian Parliament enacted the Consumer Protection Act in 1986. India is one of the countries that have exclusive authority for consumer redressal. There are today more than 2000 consumer groups, of which only about 50-60 are well organised and recognised for their work.

checks.criterion: Mentions that 24 December is observed as National Consumers' Day, when COPRA was enacted in 1986.
Mentions that there are more than 2000 consumer groups, of which only about 50-60 are well organised.

keyPoints.text: However, the consumer redressal process is becoming cumbersome, expensive and time consuming. Many a time, consumers are required to engage lawyers. In most purchases cash memos are not issued hence evidence is not easy to gather. Moreover most purchases in the market are small retail sales. Enforcement of laws that protect workers is weak, and rules for the working of markets are often not followed.
keyPoints.followUp: What problems do consumers face when they try to get justice?

checks.criterion: Names problems of the consumer redressal process: cumbersome, expensive and time consuming, needing lawyers, no cash memos as evidence, or mostly small retail sales.

keyPoints.text: COPRA was amended in the year 2019 to further strengthen consumers in India. Buying through internet is now included. If there is any service deficiency or defective product, the service provider or manufacturer is also held responsible and would be penalized or even imprisoned. Settlement of disputes through a neutral intermediary called a mediator is now encouraged at all three tiers of Consumer Commissions.
keyPoints.followUp: What changes were made to COPRA in 2019?

checks.criterion: Mentions that the 2019 amendment of COPRA includes buying through the internet.
Mentions that under the 2019 amendment, service providers or manufacturers can be penalised or imprisoned for deficient service or defective products.
Mentions that settlement through a mediator is now encouraged at all three tiers of consumer commissions.

keyPoints.text: After more than 30 years of COPRA, consumer awareness in India is spreading but slowly. Consumer movements can be effective only with the consumers' active involvement. It requires a voluntary effort and struggle involving the participation of one and all.
keyPoints.followUp: How far has consumer awareness spread, and what does the movement need to succeed?

checks.criterion: Concludes that consumer awareness is spreading slowly, and consumer movements can be effective only with consumers' active involvement and participation.

COPRA covers services too: Reji's, Abirami's and Prakash's cases were about services, and the 2019 amendment holds service providers responsible for deficient service.
